data.note:
Reflection: I misclassified proteasome inhibitor I as a microtubule stabilizer.

Evidence for stabilizer looked strong: tub_mean z +5.5 to +11.3 with tub_glcm_contrast z up to +30.4, microscopist reporting bright bundled tubulin, and atlas 8/10 stabilizer neighbours (docetaxel, epothilone B, taxol, mean sim 0.79) vs only 1x MG-132 protein-degradation neighbour at sim 0.68.

In hindsight I over-weighted cosine similarity and tubulin brightness. Proteasome inhibition causes accumulation of ubiquitinated / stabilized proteins including cytoskeletal regulators, which can secondarily increase tubulin intensity/bundling and enlarge nuclei - mimicking direct stabilization. I discounted the MG-132 neighbour and did not consider this mimicry; low-dose potency (effect already at 0.01 uM) should have broadened rather than narrowed the hypotheses.

Literature supports proteasome-dependent degradation as the true biology, e.g. proteasome inhibition stabilizing IkB-alpha and blocking NF-kB activation PMID:7957109. Identity check: CID 16760625, BBBC021 structure agrees, no ChEMBL curated mechanism.

Next time: when tubulin up plus large high-DNA nuclei co-occur, keep Protein degradation on the board despite taxane neighbours, and run ubiquitin / proteasome-activity assay as follow-up.

reflection.text:
We correctly detected a strong, reproducible phenotype: high-dose tubulin intensity and texture were extreme (e2 tub_glcm_contrast z=+30.4, tub_mean z=+11.3), visible as bundles by the microscopist (e4, e5), and already present at 0.01 uM (e8 tub_mean z=+5.5). The atlas comparison returning 8/10 Microtubule stabilizers (e6) and lower density were real signals, but they reflected morphological mimicry, not mechanism.

What misled us was the comparison and acquisition strategy. We anchored on the tubulin increase and 8/10 atlas vote while discounting the 1/10 Protein degradation neighbour in e6, the large nuclear DNA shifts (e3 nuc_dna_mean z=-6.3, e8 z=-9.0) and the non-significant dose-response (e10/e11 rho=+0.40 p=0.6). Acquiring only four single-replicate wells with no ubiquitin/proteasome-activity readout left no orthogonal test to separate direct stabilization from secondary cytoskeletal remodeling.

The unblinding to proteasome inhibitor I (PMID 7957109) reframes the tubulin bundles as a downstream consequence of proteostasis block rather than direct microtubule binding. Future runs need a proteasome-specific arm when tubulin and nuclear/DNA features co-occur.
what_was_right: Detected very strong tubulin intensity/texture elevation across doses (e2 tub_mean +11.3, contrast +30.4; e3 +7.6; e8 +5.5)
Noted reduced density/cell counts at high and mid doses (198-238 cells) consistent with proteasome-inhibitor toxicity
Recorded concurrent nuclear DNA and shape changes (nuc_dna_mean -6.3 to -9.0, nuc_eccentricity up to +11.8) that did not fit a pure taxane pattern
Atlas retained a 1/10 Protein degradation neighbour that preserved the true MOA signal
what_was_wrong: Interpreted bright bundled tubulin (e2, e4, e5) as direct microtubule stabilization, missing secondary tubulin remodeling after proteasome inhibition
Overweighted 8/10 stabilizer atlas vote (e6) and microscopist candidate label while dismissing Protein degradation at 0.03 probability
Treated early saturation at 0.01 uM (e8) and flat dose-response rho=0.40 p=0.6 (e10, e11) as confirmation instead of a warning of non-specific or off-target effect

Acquisition choice of 4 single-replicate wells with tubulin/DNA imaging only and no polyubiquitin or proteasome-activity control, plus literature search that returned 0 hits for proteasome-tubulin link (e17) without follow-up

## Hypothesis history

- after step 7: Microtubule stabilizers 0.90, Microtubule destabilizers 0.05, Protein degradation 0.03, Cholesterol-lowering 0.02
- after step 12: Microtubule stabilizers 0.92, Microtubule destabilizers 0.03, Protein degradation 0.03, Cholesterol-lowering 0.02

## Conclusion

**Microtubule stabilizers** (stated probability 0.92); key evidence e2, e4, e6, e8.

Why: Bright bundled tubulin with high atlas similarity to taxanes strongly supports stabilizer.

Next experiment if this were a real lab: Washout + phospho-histone H3 / mitotic index timecourse with live tubulin to confirm stabilized bundles and mitotic arrest reversibility.

## PI review

Verdict: approve.

Approve: evidence favors Microtubule stabilizers over runner-ups. Tubulin intensity/texture is markedly increased across doses (tub_mean z=+5.5 to +11.3; high-dose contrast z=+30.4), with bundled tubulin visually described at 0.3 and 10 uM—opposite to destabilization. Atlas is 8/10 stabilizers (mean similarity 0.792) vs 1/10 each for protein degradation and cholesterol-lowering. Cross-dose consistency mitigates single-replicate wells; the flat contrast at 1 uM and weak dose-response rho do not plausibly favor a runner-up. Probability 0.92 is calibrated.

## Unblinding

Compound: **proteasome inhibitor I** (PubChem CID [16760625](https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/16760625))

Identity check: name and BBBC021 structure agree

ChEMBL mechanisms: no curated mechanism in ChEMBL

## Verdict (computed by code)

Incorrect: agent said **Microtubule stabilizers**, BBBC021 annotates **Protein degradation**.

## Reflection

We correctly detected a strong, reproducible phenotype: high-dose tubulin intensity and texture were extreme (e2 tub_glcm_contrast z=+30.4, tub_mean z=+11.3), visible as bundles by the microscopist (e4, e5), and already present at 0.01 uM (e8 tub_mean z=+5.5). The atlas comparison returning 8/10 Microtubule stabilizers (e6) and lower density were real signals, but they reflected morphological mimicry, not mechanism.

What misled us was the comparison and acquisition strategy. We anchored on the tubulin increase and 8/10 atlas vote while discounting the 1/10 Protein degradation neighbour in e6, the large nuclear DNA shifts (e3 nuc_dna_mean z=-6.3, e8 z=-9.0) and the non-significant dose-response (e10/e11 rho=+0.40 p=0.6). Acquiring only four single-replicate wells with no ubiquitin/proteasome-activity readout left no orthogonal test to separate direct stabilization from secondary cytoskeletal remodeling.

The unblinding to proteasome inhibitor I (PMID 7957109) reframes the tubulin bundles as a downstream consequence of proteostasis block rather than direct microtubule binding. Future runs need a proteasome-specific arm when tubulin and nuclear/DNA features co-occur.

What was right:
- Detected very strong tubulin intensity/texture elevation across doses (e2 tub_mean +11.3, contrast +30.4; e3 +7.6; e8 +5.5)
- Noted reduced density/cell counts at high and mid doses (198-238 cells) consistent with proteasome-inhibitor toxicity
- Recorded concurrent nuclear DNA and shape changes (nuc_dna_mean -6.3 to -9.0, nuc_eccentricity up to +11.8) that did not fit a pure taxane pattern
- Atlas retained a 1/10 Protein degradation neighbour that preserved the true MOA signal

What was wrong or missed:
- Interpreted bright bundled tubulin (e2, e4, e5) as direct microtubule stabilization, missing secondary tubulin remodeling after proteasome inhibition
- Overweighted 8/10 stabilizer atlas vote (e6) and microscopist candidate label while dismissing Protein degradation at 0.03 probability
- Treated early saturation at 0.01 uM (e8) and flat dose-response rho=0.40 p=0.6 (e10, e11) as confirmation instead of a warning of non-specific or off-target effect
- Acquisition choice of 4 single-replicate wells with tubulin/DNA imaging only and no polyubiquitin or proteasome-activity control, plus literature search that returned 0 hits for proteasome-tubulin link (e17) without follow-up

Proposed next experiment: Side-by-side dose-response of proteasome inhibitor I vs bortezomib/MG132 vs paclitaxel with polyubiquitin staining plus proteasome activity reporter and tubulin imaging with washout to test if bundling is secondary to proteostasis block.

## Citations

Citations verified: 3/3

- PMID [7957109](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7957109/): A proteasome inhibitor prevents activation of NF-kappa B and stabilizes a newly phosphorylated form of I kappa B-alpha that is still bound to NF-kappa B. *EMBO J* (1994) — Proteasome inhibition prevents NF-kappa B activation by stabilizing a phosphorylated form of I kappa B-alpha still bound to NF-kappa B.
- PMID [12209081](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12209081/): Proteasome-dependent regulation of Syk tyrosine kinase levels in human basophils. *J Allergy Clin Immunol* (2002) — Cellular levels of Syk tyrosine kinase are regulated by proteasome-dependent degradation.
- PMID [31569723](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31569723/): Proteasome Inhibitors Suppress ErbB Family Expression through HSP90-Mediated Lysosomal Degradation. *Int J Mol Sci* (2019) — Proteasome inhibitors suppress protein expression through HSP90-mediated lysosomal degradation pathways.
